claim: Patients with severe infections caused by SARS-CoV-2 have high circulating concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Patients with severe infections caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 (known as COVID-19) have high circulating concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is a general statement about COVID-19 pathophysiology that is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Cytokine concentrations in severe COVID-19 are often not as high as in patients with classical ARDS and septic shock.
source: Although these concentrations are often not as high as in patients with classical acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and septic shock (Sinha et al., 2020), systemic inflammation is an important feature of severe COVID-19.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sinha et al., 2020.

claim: Systemic inflammation is an important feature of severe COVID-19.
source: Although these concentrations are often not as high as in patients with classical acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and septic shock (Sinha et al., 2020), systemic inflammation is an important feature of severe COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about COVID-19 pathophysiology.

claim: When severe respiratory failure necessitating mechanical ventilation emerges in COVID-19, macrophage activation syndrome involves 25% of patients.
source: It has been shown that when severe respiratory failure (SRF) necessitating mechanical ventilation (MV) emerges, two separate immune phenomena predominate in the infected host; (i) macrophage activation syndrome involving 25% patients; or (ii) complex immune dysregulation with down-regulation of the human leukocyte antigen DR on circulating monocytes, lymphopenia, and over-production of interleukin (IL)−6 by monocytes involving 75% of the patients (Giamarellos-Bourboulis et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Giamarellos-Bourboulis et al., 2020.

claim: When severe respiratory failure necessitating mechanical ventilation emerges in COVID-19, complex immune dysregulation with down-regulation of HLA-DR on circulating monocytes, lymphopenia, and over-production of IL-6 by monocytes involves 75% of patients.
source: It has been shown that when severe respiratory failure (SRF) necessitating mechanical ventilation (MV) emerges, two separate immune phenomena predominate in the infected host; (i) macrophage activation syndrome involving 25% patients; or (ii) complex immune dysregulation with down-regulation of the human leukocyte antigen DR on circulating monocytes, lymphopenia, and over-production of interleukin (IL)−6 by monocytes involving 75% of the patients (Giamarellos-Bourboulis et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Giamarellos-Bourboulis et al., 2020.

claim: Immune reactions in COVID-19 start early in patients with lower respiratory tract infection and are progressively enhanced to lead to severe respiratory failure.
source: It is hypothesized that these immune reactions start early in patients with lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) by SARS-CoV-2 and are progressively enhanced so as to lead to SRF.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis about the progression of COVID-19.

claim: Early release of IL-1 from lung epithelial cells infected by SARS-CoV-2 stimulates further cytokine production from alveolar macrophages.
source: This has been suggested to be due to the early release of IL-1 from the lung epithelial cells that are infected by the virus; IL-1 stimulates further cytokine production from alveolar macrophages (Conti et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Conti et al., 2020.

claim: Early start of anti-IL-1 anti-inflammatory treatment may prevent severe respiratory failure in COVID-19.
source: As a consequence, it is assumed that early start of anti-IL-1 anti-inflammatory treatment may prevent SRF (van de Veerdonk and Netea, 2020).
evidence: This is presented as an assumption supported by a citation to van de Veerdonk and Netea, 2020.

claim: Not all patients with LRTI by SARS-CoV-2 are in need of early treatment.
source: However, most probably not all patients with LRTI by SARS-CoV-2 are in need of early treatment and a screening tool to capture those who are likely to progress to SRF would be an asset.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about treatment strategy.

claim: Soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR) is a screening tool to identify patients likely to progress to severe respiratory failure.
source: Soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR) seems to be such a screening tool.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: suPAR concentrations above 6 ng/ml herald worsening to severe respiratory failure 14 days earlier.
source: We and others recently demonstrated that suPAR concentrations above 6 ng/ml herald worsening to SRF 14 days earlier (Rovina et al., 2020; Azam et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rovina et al., 2020 and Azam et al., 2020.

claim: The positive predictive value of suPAR above 6 ng/ml for early prediction of severe respiratory failure is 85.9%.
source: The positive predictive value for the early prediction of SRF was as high as 85.9%.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research.

claim: uPAR is anchored to the cell membranes of lung endothelial cells.
source: uPAR is anchored to the cell membranes of the lung endothelial cells.
evidence: This is stated as established biological knowledge.

claim: As a result of kallikrein activation, uPAR is cleaved and enters the systemic circulation as soluble suPAR.
source: As a result of the activation of kallikrein, uPAR is cleaved and enters the systemic circulation as the soluble counterpart suPAR (Pixley et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pixley et al., 2011.

claim: Anakinra is the recombinant soluble IL-1 receptor antagonist that blocks both IL-1α and IL-1β.
source: Anakinra is the recombinant soluble IL-1 receptor antagonist that blocks both IL-1α and IL-1β.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the drug mechanism.

claim: The first patient in the SAVE trial was enrolled on April 16, 2020.
source: The first patient was enrolled on April 16, 2020 and the last on September 12, 2020.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the trial timeline.

claim: The last patient in the SAVE trial was enrolled on September 12, 2020.
source: The first patient was enrolled on April 16, 2020 and the last on September 12, 2020.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the trial timeline.

claim: 211 patients were excluded from the SAVE trial because they had suPAR less than 6 ng/ml.
source: In all, 211 patients were excluded because they had suPAR less than 6 ng/ml; patients were followed-up and SRF developed in seven (3.3%) patients.
evidence: This is a factual statement about trial enrollment.

claim: Among 211 patients excluded for suPAR less than 6 ng/ml, severe respiratory failure developed in 7 patients (3.3%).
source: In all, 211 patients were excluded because they had suPAR less than 6 ng/ml; patients were followed-up and SRF developed in seven (3.3%) patients.
evidence: This is a factual statement about outcomes in excluded patients.

claim: 22.3% of patients receiving anakinra with SOC treatment progressed to severe respiratory failure by day 14.
source: Twenty-nine patients (22.3%; 95% CI, 16.0–30.2%) among the intent-to-treat (ITT) population receiving anakinra and SOC progressed to SRF until day 14.
evidence: This is the primary outcome data from the trial.

claim: 59.2% of parallel SOC-treated comparators progressed to severe respiratory failure by day 14.
source: The incidence of SRF among the 130 parallel SOC-treated comparators was 59.2% (n = 77) (95% CI, 50.6–67.3%, p<0.0001) (hazard ratio 0.30; 95% CI, 0.20–0.46) (Figure 1A and Table 2).
evidence: This is the primary outcome data from the comparator group, referenced in Figure 1A and Table 2.

claim: Anakinra treatment is associated with a hazard ratio of 0.30 (95% CI, 0.20–0.46) for progression to severe respiratory failure compared to standard-of-care.
source: The incidence of SRF among the 130 parallel SOC-treated comparators was 59.2% (n = 77) (95% CI, 50.6–67.3%, p<0.0001) (hazard ratio 0.30; 95% CI, 0.20–0.46) (Figure 1A and Table 2).
evidence: This is the primary outcome analysis, referenced in Figure 1A and Table 2.

claim: Anakinra treatment was the only independent variable protective from severe respiratory failure in multivariate Cox regression analysis.
source: Multivariate step-wise Cox regression analysis for variables showed that anakinra treatment was the only independent variable protective from SRF (hazard ratio 0.28; 95% CI, 0.18–0.44; p<0.0001) (Table 3).
evidence: This is the result of multivariate analysis, referenced in Table 3.

claim: 30-day mortality was 11.5% in anakinra-treated patients.
source: Mortality of participants in the SAVE trial receiving anakinra treatment after 30 days was 11.5% (95% CI, 7.1–18.2%); this was 22.3% (95% CI, 16.0–30.2%) in parallel comparators receiving SOC (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a secondary outcome from the trial, referenced in Figure 1B.

claim: 30-day mortality was 22.3% in parallel SOC comparators.
source: Mortality of participants in the SAVE trial receiving anakinra treatment after 30 days was 11.5% (95% CI, 7.1–18.2%); this was 22.3% (95% CI, 16.0–30.2%) in parallel comparators receiving SOC (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a secondary outcome from the comparator group, referenced in Figure 1B.

claim: Anakinra treatment was the only independent variable protective from 30-day mortality in multivariate Cox regression analysis.
source: Multivariate step-wise Cox regression analysis for variables showed that anakinra treatment was the only independent variable protective from 30-day mortality (hazard ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.25–0.97; p: 0.041) (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is the result of multivariate analysis for mortality.

claim: Anakinra-treated subjects experienced increase of the absolute lymphocyte count compared to SOC comparators.
source: Compared to SOC comparators, anakinra-treated subjects experienced increase of the absolute lymphocyte count and decreases of IL-6, sCD163, and sIL-2R (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a secondary outcome on biomarkers, referenced in Figure 2.

claim: Anakinra-treated subjects experienced decreases of IL-6, sCD163, and sIL-2R compared to SOC comparators.
source: Compared to SOC comparators, anakinra-treated subjects experienced increase of the absolute lymphocyte count and decreases of IL-6, sCD163, and sIL-2R (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a secondary outcome on biomarkers, referenced in Figure 2.

claim: The IL-10/IL-6 ratio of serum on day 7 was inversely associated with the absolute increase of the SOFA score on day 14 among anakinra-treated patients.
source: The IL-10/IL-6 ratio of serum (an index of the anti-inflammatory/pro-inflammatory balance in severe COVID-19 [McElvaney et al., 2020]) was inversely associated with the absolute increase of the SOFA score on day 14 among anakinra-treated patients, compatible with the anti-inflammatory effect of anakinra.
evidence: This is an analysis of biomarker associations with clinical outcomes.

claim: The IL-10/IL-6 ratio is an index of the anti-inflammatory/pro-inflammatory balance in severe COVID-19.
source: The IL-10/IL-6 ratio of serum (an index of the anti-inflammatory/pro-inflammatory balance in severe COVID-19 [McElvaney et al., 2020]) was inversely associated with the absolute increase of the SOFA score on day 14 among anakinra-treated patients, compatible with the anti-inflammatory effect of anakinra.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McElvaney et al., 2020.

claim: suPAR was increased among anakinra-treated patients on day 7 from baseline.
source: Remarkably, suPAR was increased among anakinra-treated patients on day 7 from baseline.
evidence: This is a biomarker finding from the trial.

claim: Anakinra is associated with protection against progression to severe respiratory failure even when the suPAR signal indicates an unfavorable outcome.
source: Thus, anakinra is associated with protection against progression to SRF even when the suPAR signal indicates an unfavorable outcome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the suPAR increase despite clinical benefit.

claim: The production of IL-1β on day 7 was greater among anakinra-treated patients who did not develop severe respiratory failure.
source: More precisely, the production of IL-1β and IL-10 on day 7 was greater among patients who did not develop SRF pointing toward a restoration of the ability of the PBMCs to adapt to balanced production of anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is a finding from PBMC functional studies.

claim: The production of IL-10 on day 7 was greater among anakinra-treated patients who did not develop severe respiratory failure.
source: More precisely, the production of IL-1β and IL-10 on day 7 was greater among patients who did not develop SRF pointing toward a restoration of the ability of the PBMCs to adapt to balanced production of anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is a finding from PBMC functional studies.

claim: There is a positive association between the IL-10/IL-1β ratio of production from PBMCs on day 7 with the ratio of serum IL-10/IL-6 of the same day.
source: This was further corroborated with the positive association between the IL-10/IL-1β ratio of production from PBMCs on day 7 with the ratio of serum IL-10/IL-6 of the same day (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis, referenced in Figure 3.

claim: The number of ventilator-free days until day 28 was increased with anakinra treatment.
source: The number of ventilator-free days until day 28 was increased with anakinra treatment (Table 2) and 90-day mortality was decreased (Table 2 and Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is an exploratory endpoint, referenced in Table 2.

claim: 90-day mortality was decreased with anakinra treatment.
source: The number of ventilator-free days until day 28 was increased with anakinra treatment (Table 2) and 90-day mortality was decreased (Table 2 and Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is an exploratory endpoint, referenced in Table 2 and Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: Participants of the SAVE trial were allocated to strata of lower severity by day 28 compared to propensity-matched parallel SOC comparators.
source: Participants of the SAVE trial were allocated to strata of lower severity by day 28 compared to propensity-matched parallel SOC comparators (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an exploratory endpoint on WHO-CPS, referenced in Figure 4.

claim: The overall cost of hospitalization decreased from median €2398.4 among SOC treated comparators to €1291.4 among anakinra-treated patients.
source: The overall cost of hospitalization decreased from median €2398.4 among SOC treated comparators to €1291.4 among anakinra-treated patients (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is an exploratory endpoint on cost, referenced in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The incidence of adverse events was not greater in the anakinra group than comparators, with the only exception of leukopenia having a trend to be higher in the anakinra group.
source: As shown in Table 4, the incidence of these events was not greater in the anakinra group than comparators, with the only exception of leukopenia having a trend to be higher in the anakinra group.
evidence: This is a safety analysis, referenced in Table 4.

claim: Serious adverse events were fewer among anakinra-treated patients.
source: SAEs were fewer among anakinra-treated patients.
evidence: This is a safety finding from the trial.

claim: In a retrospective analysis by Cavalli et al., 29 patients with respiratory failure and respiratory ratio below 100 mmHg were treated with high dose anakinra intravenously (5 mg/kg twice daily), and treatment was associated with clinical improvement in 72% and remarkably higher survival rate.
source: In a retrospective analysis by Cavalli et al., 29 patients with respiratory failure and respiratory ratio below 100 mmHg were treated with high dose anakinra intravenously (5 mg/kg twice daily). Treatment was associated with clinical improvement in 72% and remarkably higher survival rate (Cavalli et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: In the Ana-COVID prospective study, 52 patients with confirmed COVID-19 and bilateral lung infiltrates and oxygen saturation less than 93% were treated with 100 mg anakinra subcutaneously twice daily for 3 days followed by 100 mg subcutaneously once daily for another 7 days, achieving a 78% decrease of the composite endpoint of MV and/or death compared to 44 historical controls.
source: In the Ana-COVID prospective study, 52 patients with confirmed COVID-19 and bilateral lung infiltrates and oxygen saturation less than 93% were treated with 100 mg anakinra subcutaneously twice daily for 3 days followed by 100 mg subcutaneously once daily for another 7 days. The study had a composite endpoint much similar to the endpoint of the SAVE study; that is, MV and/or death. Anakinra treatment achieved a 78% decrease of this composite endpoint compared to 44 historical controls. However, studied comparators were not matched for co-administered medication such as azithromycin and hydroxychloroquine (Huet et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: In a retrospective study, 12 patients with COVID pneumonia and increased C-reactive protein were intravenously treated with anakinra 300 mg/day and none died.
source: In a retrospective study, 12 patients with COVID pneumonia and increased C-reactive protein were intravenously treated with anakinra 300 mg/day; none died (Cauchois et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: The best candidates for anakinra treatment are patients with high likelihood of severe respiratory failure as defined by increased suPAR.
source: In this respect, the SAVE study gives guidance: the best candidates are patients with high likelihood of SRF as defined by increased suPAR; anakinra presented one well-acceptable safety profile at the standard subcutaneous daily dose of 100 mg.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SAVE trial results.

claim: Anakinra presented a well-acceptable safety profile at the standard subcutaneous daily dose of 100 mg.
source: In this respect, the SAVE study gives guidance: the best candidates are patients with high likelihood of SRF as defined by increased suPAR; anakinra presented one well-acceptable safety profile at the standard subcutaneous daily dose of 100 mg.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the safety data of the SAVE trial.

claim: Anakinra treatment was associated with a reset of the pro- versus anti-inflammatory balance of the host.
source: An important additional finding of the SAVE trial is that it provides mechanistic insight into the biological effects of anakinra: the treatment was associated with a reset of the pro- versus anti-inflammatory balance of the host.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the biomarker data.

claim: The production capacity of PBMCs for the anti-inflammatory IL-10 was increased with anakinra treatment.
source: The production capacity of PMBCs for the anti-inflammatory IL-10 was increased and this was reflected by the serum IL-10/IL-6 ratio.
evidence: This is a finding from PBMC functional studies.

claim: The serum IL-10/IL-6 ratio was inversely associated with the absolute change of SOFA score.
source: The described reset in the production capacity of the PBMCs was linked to clinical benefit since the serum IL-10/IL-6 ratio was inversely associated with the absolute change of SOFA score.
evidence: This is a correlation analysis linking biomarkers to clinical outcomes.

claim: Anakinra treatment decreased the elevated serum concentrations of sCD163 and sIL2-R that are biomarkers of macrophage activation.
source: Anakinra treatment also decreased the elevated serum concentrations of sCD163 and sIL2-R that are biomarkers of macrophage activation (Bleesing et al., 2007; Rubin, 1990).
evidence: This is a biomarker finding supported by citations about the markers' significance.

claim: sCD163 and sIL2-R are biomarkers of macrophage activation.
source: Anakinra treatment also decreased the elevated serum concentrations of sCD163 and sIL2-R that are biomarkers of macrophage activation (Bleesing et al., 2007; Rubin, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bleesing et al., 2007 and Rubin, 1990.

claim: Patients with COVID-19 who deteriorate have characteristics of macrophage activation.
source: It was noted before that patients with COVID-19 who deteriorate have characteristics of macrophage activation (Zhou et al., 2020); the decrease of these biomarkers indicates attenuation of macrophage activation among anakinra-treated patients.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: The decrease of sCD163 and sIL2-R biomarkers indicates attenuation of macrophage activation among anakinra-treated patients.
source: It was noted before that patients with COVID-19 who deteriorate have characteristics of macrophage activation (Zhou et al., 2020); the decrease of these biomarkers indicates attenuation of macrophage activation among anakinra-treated patients.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the biomarker changes observed in the trial.

claim: Recent data suggest early activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in severe COVID-19.
source: Recent data suggest early activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in severe COVID-19; the formation of the end product caspase-1 was enhanced among patients who had unfavorable outcome.
evidence: This is stated as recent findings about COVID-19 pathophysiology.

claim: The formation of caspase-1 was enhanced among COVID-19 patients who had unfavorable outcome.
source: Recent data suggest early activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in severe COVID-19; the formation of the end product caspase-1 was enhanced among patients who had unfavorable outcome.
evidence: This is stated as recent findings about COVID-19 pathophysiology.

claim: Stimulation of human monocytes with SARS-CoV-2 could not induce production of IL-1β and priming was needed.
source: Stimulation of human monocytes with SARS-CoV-2 could not induce production of IL-1β and priming was needed.
evidence: This is stated as a finding about SARS-CoV-2 effects on monocytes.

claim: Over-produced IL-1β in COVID-19 is derived from the cleavage of pro-IL-1β induced by SARS-CoV-2.
source: Findings suggest that over-produced IL-1β is derived from the cleavage of pro-IL-1β induced by SARS-CoV-2 (Rodrigues et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rodrigues et al., 2021.

claim: Anakinra may inhibit the early production of IL-1β following NLRP3 activation due to the autocrine effects of IL-1.
source: While anakinra treatment is meant to inhibit IL-1 bioactivity through blocking of its receptor, it may also inhibit the early production of IL-1β following NLRP3 activation due to the autocrine effects of IL-1 (Dinarello et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation supported by a citation to Dinarello et al., 1987.

claim: Anakinra inhibits IL-1α.
source: Anakinra also inhibits IL-1α.
evidence: This is stated as a known mechanism of anakinra.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection is suggested to cause massive release of IL-1α followed by sensing from monocytes and tissue macrophages and further activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome leading to perpetuation of the pro-inflammatory responses.
source: SARS-CoV-2 infection is suggested to cause massive release of IL-1α followed by sensing from monocytes and tissue macrophages and further activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome leading to perpetuation of the pro-inflammatory responses (Cavalli et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cavalli et al., 2021.

claim: Anakinra is protective in patients receiving dexamethasone.
source: Although this is not a preset endpoint, post hoc analysis shows that anakinra is also protective in patients receiving dexamethasone (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a post hoc analysis finding, referenced in Appendix 1—table 2.

claim: Early suPAR-guided anakinra treatment decreased severe respiratory failure and restored the pro-/anti-inflammatory balance.
source: Conclusions:Early suPAR-guided anakinra decreased SRF and restored the pro-/anti-inflammatory balance.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the trial results.

claim: Early suPAR-guided anakinra treatment can prevent severe respiratory failure of COVID-19.
source: Background:It was studied if early suPAR-guided anakinra treatment can prevent severe respiratory failure (SRF) of COVID-19.
evidence: This is the study objective stated in the abstract.

claim: 22.3% with anakinra treatment and 59.2% comparators progressed into severe respiratory failure (hazard ratio, 0.30; 95% CI, 0.20–0.46).
source: Results:22.3% with anakinra treatment and 59.2% comparators (hazard ratio, 0.30; 95% CI, 0.20–0.46) progressed into SRF; 30-day mortality was 11.5% and 22.3% respectively (hazard ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.25–0.97).
evidence: This is the primary outcome stated in the abstract.

claim: 30-day mortality was 11.5% with anakinra treatment and 22.3% in comparators (hazard ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.25–0.97).
source: Results:22.3% with anakinra treatment and 59.2% comparators (hazard ratio, 0.30; 95% CI, 0.20–0.46) progressed into SRF; 30-day mortality was 11.5% and 22.3% respectively (hazard ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.25–0.97).
evidence: This is a secondary outcome stated in the abstract.

claim: Anakinra was associated with decrease in circulating IL-6, sCD163 and sIL2-R.
source: Anakinra was associated with decrease in circulating interleukin (IL)−6, sCD163 and sIL2-R; IL-10/IL-6 ratio on day 7 was inversely associated with SOFA score; patients were allocated to less severe WHO-CPS strata.
evidence: This is a secondary outcome stated in the abstract.

claim: IL-10/IL-6 ratio on day 7 was inversely associated with SOFA score.
source: Anakinra was associated with decrease in circulating interleukin (IL)−6, sCD163 and sIL2-R; IL-10/IL-6 ratio on day 7 was inversely associated with SOFA score; patients were allocated to less severe WHO-CPS strata.
evidence: This is a secondary outcome stated in the abstract.

claim: Anakinra-treated patients were allocated to less severe WHO-CPS strata.
source: Anakinra was associated with decrease in circulating interleukin (IL)−6, sCD163 and sIL2-R; IL-10/IL-6 ratio on day 7 was inversely associated with SOFA score; patients were allocated to less severe WHO-CPS strata.
evidence: This is an exploratory outcome stated in the abstract.

claim: The restoration of the pro-inflammatory/anti-inflammatory balance is proposed as the mechanism of anakinra action.
source: In conclusion, we propose a novel strategy using suPAR as an early biomarker that can effectively identify those patients at high risk for SRF. In these patients, prophylactic treatment with regular doses of anakinra is associated with prevention of the incidence of SRF. The restoration of the pro-inflammatory/anti-inflammatory balance is proposed as the mechanism of anakinra action.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion drawn from the biomarker and functional data.
